one_liner: Mesh library whose lossless vertex codec, misused on float pixels, beat OpenEXR ZIP: 1.4x encode, 3.1x decode, 7% smaller.
what_it_does: meshoptimizer is an MIT C/C++ library for GPU mesh optimization; one of its parts is a lossless codec for arrays of fixed-size records (meshopt_encodeVertexBufferLevel / meshopt_decodeVertexBuffer). The catalogued benchmark treats each pixel of an interleaved half/float image as a 'vertex', encodes 16K-pixel chunks in parallel and optionally runs zstd over each chunk. There is no image API, file format or channel metadata: the caller writes its own container (the harness's MOPF header plus a chunk-size table), so this is a building block for internal storage, not a replacement for OpenEXR files.
how_it_is_fast: Records are processed in blocks of up to 256 (8 KB / record size). Each block is transposed into one byte stream per byte position and delta-coded against the previous record (byte delta, 16-bit delta or, at level 3, 32-bit XOR with a rotation, chosen once per 4-byte lane at levels 2-3) with zigzag mapping. Each 16-byte group of deltas is then bit-packed at 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 bits with a sentinel-plus-literal escape for outliers, chosen per group with 2-bit headers. There is no entropy coder or match search, so decoding is table-driven shuffles: SSSE3 (picked by cpuid on MSVC x64), NEON on arm64, Wasm SIMD and an opt-in AVX-512 path, about 8 GB/s on a 16-thread Ryzen 9 5950X and 14.8 GB/s on an M4 Max in the measured run. Encoding is scalar C++.
when_to_use: Internal caches or intermediate files of half/float render buffers, AOVs, lightmaps or simulation fields where you control both writer and reader and do not need interop (the harness author's own recommendation).
Decode-bound pipelines: the decode stayed at 7.9-8.1 GB/s (Ryzen 9 5950X) and 14.7-14.8 GB/s (M4 Max) across levels 0-3, versus 2.5 and 6.0 GB/s for EXR ZIP level 4.
Layered images with many interleaved channels (the test set had up to 37 channels per pixel), as long as one pixel fits in 256 bytes.
When you want a better ratio and can afford a bit more encode time: stacking zstd level 1 on level 2 raised the ratio from 2.011 to 2.248 at 1.53 GB/s encode and 6.7 GB/s decode on the Ryzen.
Code-size-sensitive builds: the harness measured +26 KB of executable for the codec (+431 KB with zstd) versus +308 KB for EXR HTJ2K and +6017 KB for libjxl.
when_not_to_use: Files other tools must read: there is no image format, and the 'MOP' container exists only in the benchmark repository. Use OpenEXR (ZIP, or HTJ2K via OpenJPH) for interchange.
Maximum lossless ratio: libjxl effort 7 reached 2.180 and effort 8 2.434 on the same files (at 0.05 and 0.007 GB/s encode), and plain Mop2 stops at 2.011.
Data without left-to-right correlation: the only predictor is the previous record in memory order (no vertical or 2D prediction), and the README warns that unordered input compresses poorly.
Records over 256 bytes or not a multiple of 4: the API asserts on both, so callers must pad (the harness zero-pads, which costs a copy per chunk) or split wide pixels into several streams.

Data that must stay readable by glTF EXT_meshopt_compression decoders or meshoptimizer older than v0.23: the benchmark used vertex format version 1, which those cannot decode; pin version 0 if needed (levels then have no effect).

integration.form: static lib by default (CMake, MESHOPT_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS option) or source-drop: the codec is src/vertexcodec.cpp plus the C-compatible header src/meshoptimizer.h
integration.dependencies: none (zstd only if you add the optional second pass yourself)
integration.min_toolchain: any mainstream C++ compiler; CMake 3.5+ if using CMake; the README says the sources build without special options or warnings; the benchmark used MSVC 2022 17.14 and Xcode clang 16
integration.platforms: any; SIMD decode on x86/x64 (SSSE3+POPCNT, runtime cpuid fallback on MSVC and GCC/clang), AVX-512 VBMI2 only when compiled in, NEON on ARM/AArch64, Wasm SIMD; scalar fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Encode and decode use only stack buffers and can run concurrently on separate buffers (the harness runs 16 chunks at once); meshopt_encodeVertexVersion sets a global and must not race with encoders, so pass the version argument explicitly as the harness does.

gotchas: Channel modes are chosen per 4-byte lane of the record, so a float channel straddling a 4-byte boundary (possible in mixed half/float layouts) or an odd count of half channels gets a worse delta mode; reorder channels so each 4-byte lane holds one float or two halves.
The decoder does not store the record count or size: the caller must keep vertex_count and vertex_size next to the payload (the harness keeps them in its own header).
The decoder is safe on untrusted input but 'may produce garbage data' on malformed streams; check the return code and add your own checksum if integrity matters.

The measured build was v0.25. The v1.2 release notes say a new mostly branchless SSSE3 decoder is about 20-45% faster on Intel/AMD and AVX-512 adds about 10%, so the current v1.3 should decode faster on x86 than measured; this has not been re-benchmarked in the harness.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued image codecs only OpenJPH (as OpenEXR HTJ2K) and LERC target float or raster data; pick meshoptimizer over HTJ2K when you do not need a standard file and want speed (HTJ2K_256 in the same run: ratio 1.947 at 0.709/1.045 GB/s on the Ryzen versus Mop2 2.011 at 1.600/7.861 GB/s). The 8-bit lossless codecs (QOI, fpng, fpnge, QOIR) do not handle half/float pixels at all.
verified_claims_summary: Aras Pranckevicius's public harness (aras-p/test_exr_htj2k_jxl) round-tripped ten float EXR images (3122 MB raw) in memory with a bit-exact check, best of 3 runs, 16 threads on both sides, Release builds with MSVC 2022 17.14 on a Ryzen 9 5950X and Xcode clang 16 on an M4 Max. meshoptimizer v0.25 level 2 reached ratio 2.011 at 1.600 GB/s encode and 7.861 GB/s decode versus OpenEXR 3.4.0 ZIP level 4 at 1.873, 1.172 and 2.526 GB/s on the Ryzen (1.37x and 3.1x, derived), and 3.104/14.808 versus 1.723/5.993 GB/s on the M4 Max (1.80x and 2.47x, derived).
status_note: Very actively maintained (v1.3 released September 2026, last commit 2026-09-28, about 8.5k stars, 4 open issues), MIT-licensed and packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, Arch, FreeBSD, Nix, vcpkg and Conan; copyable, but the image use is off-label and the container format is yours to write.
measurement_notes: Read the harness code behind the numbers. main.cpp times SaveMopFile/LoadMopFile against OpenEXR's OutputFile/InputFile writing to and reading from in-memory streams, sums times over the ten files and keeps the best of three runs; CompareImages checks fp16 channels bit for bit and fp32 channels by value (so +0/-0 or NaN payload differences would not be caught, irrelevant for a byte-exact codec). SanitizePixelValues flushes fp16 subnormals to zero for every codec before the test. The thread count is the physical core count (16 on both machines); the Mop path uses a parallel-for over chunks, OpenEXR its global thread pool. The OpenEXR side also pays for converting its scanline/planar layout to the interleaved buffer, which the Mop container avoids by storing interleaved pixels; that cost is part of what 'faster than EXR ZIP' means here. The Mop wrapper's per-thread padding buffers came after meshoptimizer's author opened PR #3 on the harness ('~doubles decoding performance on Windows' by avoiding allocation contention and page faults); the harness owner closed it and implemented the same idea himself. That is a fair wrapper fix rather than library tuning and the run is still public and reproducible, so it does not affect the A tier, but the harness is not entirely independent of the library author (he also merged PR #1, a Linux build fix). zstd return codes are not checked in the wrapper; the round-trip check would catch a failure. No correctness bug or measurement flaw found behind the catalogued numbers.
